title: Elevator System
summary: A state-machine-plus-scheduling case study across multiple concurrent elevators, where SCAN/LOOK dispatch and starvation-avoidance are the real interview.

slides.markdown:
The elevator system is system-design LLD's favorite test of scheduling thinking, not just state
machines — anyone can model one elevator as idle/movingUp/movingDown/doorOpen. What separates a
strong answer is the `ElevatorController`'s dispatch algorithm: which of several elevators serves
a new request, and in what order each elevator serves its own queued requests, given that naive
"nearest elevator" and "first-come-first-served" both fail in predictable ways.

Get `Elevator`, `ElevatorController`, `Request`, and each elevator's own state machine sketched
fast, then spend the bulk of the round on SCAN/LOOK scheduling and the scoring function that
assigns requests.

Scope it as: **multiple elevators** serve **multiple floors**; requests arrive two ways — an
**external call** (a hallway up/down button) and an **internal destination** (a floor button
pressed inside a car). The system decides which elevator answers each external call and how each
elevator orders its own stops.

Non-goal: full building-traffic prediction — anticipating a morning up-rush and pre-positioning
cars — a real, valuable extension worth naming, but out of scope for getting the core scheduling
model right first.

slides.sectionTitle: Core entities: Elevator, ElevatorController, Request, Floor, Door
slides.markdown:
`Elevator` (current floor, direction, door state, its own queue of destinations),
`ElevatorController` (owns all elevators, receives external calls, assigns them), `Request`
(either an external call — floor plus desired direction — or an internal destination — just a
floor), `Floor`, and `Door`.

The entity worth calling out: `Request` as one type covering two different origins. An internal
destination and an external call end up in the same per-elevator queue once assigned, but arrive
through different entry points — keeping `Request` as one shape with an origin tag avoids
duplicating the queueing logic for each.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: class diagram for elevators, controller, request types
slides.markdown:
![ElevatorController managing Elevator queues of Request objects](assets/elevator-class-diagram.svg)

`ElevatorController` is the only thing that talks to more than one `Elevator` at a time — an
individual `Elevator` only ever knows about its own queue and its own state, never about its
siblings. That boundary is what keeps the scheduling algorithm, which lives in the controller,
separable from each elevator's own movement logic.

assets.alt: ElevatorController managing Elevator queues of Request objects

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: one elevator's own state machine
slides.markdown:
![Elevator door state machine with interruptible doorOpen](assets/elevator-door-states.svg)

`doorOpen` being interruptible matters in practice: a passenger holding the door, or a new call at
the current floor, has to extend or reset the open state rather than the elevator slamming shut on
a fixed timer regardless of what's happening.

assets.alt: Elevator door state machine with interruptible doorOpen

slides.sectionTitle: The hard part: the scheduling algorithm itself
slides.markdown:
Two decisions look similar but are genuinely different: **which elevator** serves a new external
call (the controller's job), and **in what order** a single elevator serves its own already-queued
requests (each elevator's own job). Conflating them is the most common mistake — a good
per-elevator ordering doesn't help if the controller keeps assigning every call to the same
elevator.

Both need a real algorithm, not "whichever's closest" or "whichever's queue is shortest" — those
intuitions are exactly what the next few slides show failing.

An elevator moving up should keep serving up-requests in floor order until it has none left ahead
of it, then reverse — not jump back down for whichever request arrived earliest. This is **SCAN**
(sweep to the end, like a disk head) or its refinement **LOOK** (reverse as soon as there are no
more requests ahead, without sweeping all the way to the last floor).

The payoff: passengers already being served in the current direction never get skipped for a
request that merely arrived first, and the elevator's total travel distance for a given request
set is far lower than jumping around by arrival order.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: a scheduling decision across 3 elevators
slides.markdown:
![Cost scoring three elevators for a floor 6 request](assets/elevator-cost-scoring.svg)

Distance alone would pick whichever elevator happens to be numerically closest, even if it's
moving away from floor 6 or already packed — the score has to combine distance *with* direction
match and load, which is exactly what the next slide's `assignRequest` does.

assets.alt: Cost scoring three elevators for a floor 6 request

slides.sectionTitle: Concurrency: mid-move requests and duplicate button presses
slides.markdown:
Two things can happen at once here: new requests arriving while an elevator is mid-move, and two
floor-panel presses hitting the controller at the same instant — a passenger double-tapping a
button, or an already-lit hallway button pressed again.

The queue insert (`addRequest`) and the cost-scoring read (`assignRequest`) both touch an
elevator's mutable state, so they need to stay consistent under concurrent access — typically a
per-elevator lock around queue mutation, plus an idempotent request-id (floor, direction, and a
dedup window) so a repeated press doesn't queue the same stop twice.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: centralized global optimization vs decentralized bidding
slides.markdown:
| | Centralized controller | Decentralized bidding |
|---|---|---|
| How a request is assigned | controller scores every elevator, picks the minimum | each elevator computes its own cost and "bids"; lowest bid wins |
| Optimality | can consider the whole system's state at once | each elevator only reasons about itself, can miss a globally better assignment |
| Fault isolation | controller is a single point of failure for assignment | one elevator's logic failing doesn't affect how others bid |
| Complexity | one place to get the scoring algorithm right | same algorithm runs independently per elevator, harder to keep consistent |

**How to decide:** centralized wins when you can afford the controller as critical infrastructure
(most real installations do); decentralized appeals when elevators must keep functioning
independently if the shared controller is down.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: always nearest-elevator-by-distance, starving far requests
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Just assign every request to whichever elevator is numerically closest right
now — simplest thing that could work."

**Why it's wrong:** in a busy building, an elevator far from a given floor can keep losing out to
closer elevators indefinitely as new, closer requests keep arriving — the far request waits
forever even though it arrived first. This is starvation, invisible in a light-traffic demo, then
very visible in production.

**Correct model:** the scoring function must include a wait-time factor that grows the longer a
request waits, so cost eventually favors it regardless of distance — covered concretely in the
interview slides.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: reversing direction mid-queue instead of finishing the sweep
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "As soon as any new request arrives that's technically closer, reverse and go
get it."

**Why it's wrong:** this produces the zig-zag failure mode — an elevator that keeps reversing for
each newly-closer request never makes steady progress on the requests it already committed to
serving, and every existing passenger's ride gets longer with each interruption.

**Correct model:** finish all requests in the current direction (the LOOK discipline from earlier)
before reversing — a new request in the opposite direction waits for the current sweep to end, a
bounded, predictable delay instead of an unbounded zig-zag.

slides.sectionTitle: Extending to a freight elevator with capacity/weight limits
slides.markdown:
A freight elevator adds one real constraint: `Elevator.canAccept(request)` gains a load/weight
check, so a request that would overload the car is rejected or deferred rather than queued
blindly. The scheduling algorithm itself — LOOK ordering, cost-based assignment — is unchanged; it
just now has one more precondition before a request is accepted at all.

This is a good sign the design is factored well: a materially different physical constraint plugs
in as a guard clause, not a rewrite of the scheduler.

slides.sectionTitle: Extending to multi-car dispatch (double-deck / express-local zoning)
slides.markdown:
Some buildings zone elevators — express cars skip a range of lower floors, local cars serve every
floor, or double-deck cars serve two floors per stop. The controller's job changes from "which
elevator among all of them" to "which elevator among the subset that can actually serve this
floor."

I'd model this by having each `Elevator` expose a `servableFloors` set, and having
`ElevatorController` partition elevators by that set *before* scoring — an express request only
ever gets scored against express cars. The scoring function itself doesn't change; it's just
applied to a pre-filtered candidate list.
